title: Church hurt
hook: many have been wounded by Christians; healing may take time and distance

segments.voice: Yesterday: judgment begins at the house of God, and Zacchaeus paid it back fourfold. Your line was repent.

A woman drives past the church she grew up in. Same red door. Same sign out front with the sermon title in plastic letters. She hasn't been inside for years, and her stomach still tightens at the sight of it. Somebody in there once told her something about herself, and about God, that she's still trying to unhear. Friends ask when she'll go back, as if it were a cold she ought to be over. Some people carry wounds that came from Christians, in a place that was meant to be safe.

Year one met this with a bruised reed; today goes further. Ezekiel has a whole chapter on it. God speaks against the shepherds of Israel, the leaders meant to care for the people, and the charges are specific: "The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken." Then the verdict: "with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them." The text doesn't scold the sheep for scattering. God says what he will do himself: "I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken." Some sheep didn't wander off. They were pushed. Matthew borrows Isaiah's words to describe Jesus: "A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench." A reed already bent, a lamp wick barely smoking: care that goes slowly with damaged things. And the Teacher in Ecclesiastes, listing the seasons of a life, includes "a time to heal." Healing has its own season, and it isn't rushed. For some people healing means going back to church, sometimes a different one. For some it means a long season away. Some never go back. Some readers draw a gentle way of standing beside a hurt person from these texts: no rushing, no arguing them back, no turning their pain into a debate about defending the institution. Bind up, and let them set the pace.
screen: `A BRUISED REED SHALL HE NOT BREAK.`

segments.voice: Suppose a friend sits down across from you and says, a church hurt me, and notice the first thing you want to say: an explanation, a defense. Set it down like a heavy bag, and just listen; if the friend is you, listen to yourself the same way, and if you pray, ask that they be bound up gently, at their own pace. If the hurt included abuse, or ever feels too heavy, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Church hurt. Wounds that come from a church or from Christians. In Ezekiel, God sides with the sheep that were driven away.
Your line: healing takes time. Ezekiel's God seeks the ones driven away. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-five, done.

howItsDone: Some Christians who have been hurt in church step away for a season, find a different congregation, or work through it with a counselor or a trusted pastor; some churches run listening sessions or support for people who were harmed.

fork.setup: in Ezekiel 34, the sheep are scattered, some of them driven away by their own shepherds. what does God say he will do?
options: blame the sheep for wandering off.
seek them, bring them back, and bind up the broken.
leave them to find their own way home.
fork.reveal: "I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken." the anger falls on the shepherds, not the sheep.

what a scholar hears: Matthew applies Isaiah's bruised reed and smoking flax to Jesus: a care that won't snap what's already bent.

chat.says: A church really hurt me. Everyone says just come back. Do I have to go back right away?
options: No. Ezekiel's God binds up the ones driven away, and there's a time to heal, at your pace.
Yes. Ezekiel scolds the scattered sheep for leaving, so going back fast is best.
Yes. A bruised reed has to be broken off before it can grow back strong.
chat.meaning: In Ezekiel, God sides with the sheep driven away and binds up the broken, and Ecclesiastes keeps a time to heal. Healing isn't rushed.

Ezekiel.meaning: a prophet who spoke against careless shepherds

bruised reed.meaning: a reed already bent, but not snapped

Ecclesiastes.meaning: a Bible book of wisdom spoken by the Teacher

notes: Index hook says 'many have been wounded by Christians'; the lesson avoids the 'many' claim ('some people carry wounds'). Keeper may want to soften the index hook.
Ezekiel 34 is addressed to Israel's rulers ('shepherds of Israel'); the lesson applies it by analogy to church leaders. Confirm the application is fair.
Matthew 12:18–21 quotes Isaiah 42:1–4; 'borrowing Isaiah's words' is the lesson's phrasing.
The hook's scene is invented and names no church or tradition.
